title: Winter layoffs for Ontario crews: ROEs, recall dates and spring
seo_title: Seasonal layoff in Ontario construction: ROEs and recalls
description: Laying off an Ontario crew for winter? ROE deadlines, temporary layoff limits, construction and landscaping rules, final pay and spring recalls.
excerpt: For exterior crews the season ends with layoffs, and the paperwork has deadlines. What Service Canada and Ontario's ESA guide say about ROEs, temporary layoffs and final pay, plus how to plan spring recalls.
image_alt: Pickup with a ladder rack and two shovels idling on a snowy residential street at dawn
body_html:
Short answer: When a crew member has had, or is expected to have, 7 consecutive calendar days with no work and no insurable earnings from you, Service Canada calls it an interruption of earnings, and you must issue a Record of Employment by a deadline set by how you file and how often you pay. In Ontario, a layoff past the temporary limits counts as a termination; construction and landscaping have special rules.

Checked against Service Canada and ontario.ca pages on November 17, 2026. This is general information, not legal or tax advice; confirm with your accountant or lawyer.

The last driveway is sealed, the last posts are set and the forecast says snow. For an exterior crew, that can be when layoffs start, and the paperwork that comes with them has dates attached. This post walks through what Service Canada and Ontario's Employment Standards Act (ESA) guide say, then gives you a checklist for the last day and a plan for getting your people back in spring.

Temporary layoff or termination?

The ESA guide's termination chapter sets the basic limit for a temporary layoff at not more than 13 weeks of layoff in any period of 20 consecutive weeks. A layoff can run longer and still count as temporary only under conditions and limits the guide lists. Read those conditions and limits on the page itself before you plan around them.

Two more points from the same chapter matter here. A week of lay-off is a week in which the employee earned less than half of what they would normally earn in a week. And if a layoff runs longer than a temporary layoff, the employer is considered to have terminated the employment.

Example: say a crew member's last day is Friday, December 11, 2026, and they earn nothing from you after that. Thirteen weeks from Monday, December 14 runs to mid-March 2027. If you don't expect to have work for them until April, the 13-week line falls before your start date, so read the listed conditions closely and talk to your lawyer before you pick a recall date.

Ask your lawyer one more thing before the last day: whether each person's employment contract allows layoffs.

Construction employees

The same chapter lists construction employees, and employees on temporary layoff, among the groups not entitled to notice of termination or termination pay. The construction exemption also covers employees who do off-site work and are commonly associated in work or collective bargaining with employees at the construction site. Ontario also publishes a construction special-rules page; check it against the type of work your crew does.

Landscape gardeners

Ontario's special rules for landscape gardeners cover work maintaining or changing land and gardens for aesthetic purposes. They do not cover building retaining walls for structural purposes, installing lighting systems, or spraying roads and industrial sites for weeds. Landscape gardeners are not entitled to daily or weekly limits on hours of work, overtime pay, or public holidays and public holiday pay. That page does not list termination pay as a landscape gardener exemption.

So a hardscape crew that builds structural walls one week and plants beds the next needs a closer look. Decide person by person whether the construction page or the landscaping page fits, and confirm it with your lawyer before anyone's last day.

Records of Employment: the trigger and the deadlines

Service Canada's ROE guide says an interruption of earnings happens when an employee has had, or is expected to have, 7 consecutive calendar days with no work and no insurable earnings from the employer. The guide gives layoffs as an example. You must issue an ROE each time an interruption of earnings happens, or when Service Canada asks for one.

The deadline depends on whether you file electronically or on paper, and on how often you pay:

ROE deadlines as the Service Canada ROE guide states them
How you issuePay periodsDeadline
ElectronicWeekly, biweekly or semi-monthlyUp to 5 calendar days after the end of the pay period in which the interruption of earnings occurs
ElectronicMonthly, or 13 pay periods a yearThe earlier of 5 calendar days after that pay period ends, or 15 calendar days after the first day of the interruption
PaperAs set out in the guideWithin 5 calendar days of the first day of the interruption of earnings, or of the day you become aware of it

The guide also covers special situations for part-time, on-call and casual workers, and exceptions to the seven-day rule. If anyone on your crew fits those, check the full guide or ask whoever runs your payroll.

Final pay and vacation pay

When employment ends, the ESA guide's payment of wages chapter says the employer must pay outstanding wages, including vacation pay, by the later of 7 days after the employment ends or what would normally have been the employee's next regular pay day.

The vacation chapter sets vacation pay at least 4% of the gross wages (excluding any vacation pay) earned in the 12-month vacation entitlement year for employees with less than five years of employment, and at least 6% for those with five or more years. When employment ends, unpaid vacation pay is due within seven days or on what would have been the next pay day, whichever is later.

Note what those deadlines are tied to: employment ending. This post does not answer whether accrued vacation pay has to be paid out at the start of a temporary layoff. Ask your accountant or lawyer before the last pay run of the season.

What to tell each crew member in writing

A short written note to each person, handed over or emailed before their last day, keeps everyone working from the same dates. Have your lawyer look over the wording once, then reuse it. Cover:

  • Their last day of work and the pay period it falls in.
  • That this is a layoff, and when you expect to call them back, written as an expected date or range, not a promise.
  • When their final pay and any outstanding amounts will be paid, and that you will issue their ROE.
  • How you will reach them: confirm their phone number, email and mailing address.
  • Who to contact with questions: [Your name], [Business name], [phone], [email].
  • What to tell you while they're off: a new number or address, or that they have taken other work.
  • Company gear to return: keys, fuel cards, tools and safety gear.

Planning spring recalls

Before you build the list, check each person's contract, and any collective agreement, for what it says about recall. Then work through it:

  1. Who: list each person, their role and any ticket or licence they hold, in the order you plan to call them.
  2. When: set a target date for each, checked against the 13-week mark from their first week of layoff and against your first booked jobs.
  3. Rate: write down the rate and pay basis (hourly, per-day, per-project) you will offer, so the call is about a start date, not a number.
  4. How: note how you will reach them and the date you need an answer by.
  5. Backup: if someone can't come back, who is next.

Tie the dates to real work. When a spring quote is accepted, check who on the list that job needs, and call them with the start date in hand.

Keep it together

Put the season's crew paperwork in one place before the holidays:

  • Hours and pay for each person, by job, through their last day.
  • A copy of every ROE you issued and the date you issued it.
  • The written note each person received, and the date.
  • Final pay and vacation pay records.
  • The recall list, with current contact details.

Hours by job do double duty: they also feed next year's pricing. Job costing for contractors: see each job's real margin lays out a plain method to track labour, materials, subs and receipts per job. T4 slips come next, and the Ontario contractor year-end checklist for 2026 is a December checklist that includes T4 and T5018 slips.

faq.q: When do I have to issue a Record of Employment after a layoff?
faq.a: Service Canada's ROE guide says an interruption of earnings happens when an employee has had, or is expected to have, 7 consecutive calendar days with no work and no insurable earnings from the employer, and gives layoffs as an example. Electronic ROEs for weekly, biweekly or semi-monthly pay are due up to 5 calendar days after the end of the pay period in which the interruption occurs. For monthly pay or 13 pay periods a year, the deadline is the earlier of 5 calendar days after that pay period ends or 15 calendar days after the first day of the interruption. Paper ROEs are due within 5 calendar days of the first day of the interruption, or of the day you become aware of it. Check the full guide for part-time, on-call and casual workers and for exceptions to the seven-day rule.

A longer layoff can still count as temporary only under conditions and limits the guide lists. A week of lay-off is a week in which the employee earned less than half of what they would normally earn in a week. If a layoff runs longer than a temporary layoff, the employer is considered to have terminated the employment. Read the conditions on the ontario.ca termination page and confirm your situation with your lawyer.

faq.q: Do construction employees get termination pay in Ontario?
faq.a: The ESA guide lists construction employees, and employees on temporary layoff, among the groups not entitled to notice of termination or termination pay. The construction exemption also covers employees who do off-site work and are commonly associated in work or collective bargaining with employees at the construction site. Landscape gardeners have a separate special-rules page, and that page does not list termination pay as a landscape gardener exemption. Check which page fits each worker and confirm with your lawyer.

faq.q: How should I plan spring recalls for seasonal workers?
faq.a: Start by checking each person's contract, and any collective agreement, for what it says about recall. Then build a list: who you plan to call and in what order, a target date for each checked against the 13-week temporary layoff mark and your first booked jobs, the rate and pay basis you will offer, how you will reach them and when you need an answer, and a backup for anyone who can't come back. This is general information, not legal advice.
